sermon:
## The Letter He Did Not Want to Write
*When the threat is already inside the room*

**Text:** Jude 1–4 · **Supporting:** Acts 20:29–30 · Galatians 1:6–7 · 2 Peter 2:1 · 1 Corinthians 11:19

Jude sat down to write one letter and was forced to write another. He tells us this himself, which is a strange thing for a man to admit at the start of a short and urgent note. He had a subject he loved and a subject he dreaded, and the one he dreaded won.

**He wanted to write about what we share, and could not**

Read the seam in the letter where the plan breaks. "Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 3). Notice what he wanted. He wanted to write about the salvation we hold together — the warm letter, the shared inheritance, the joy that binds a brother to a brother. That is the letter every pastor wants to write. The one about what we have, not the one about what threatens it.

He did not get to write it. The word he uses is the word a man uses when an emergency reorders his day. It was necessary. Something had already happened that made the warm letter a luxury he could no longer afford. He had to set down the thing he loved and pick up the thing he feared, because the danger was not coming. It was here.

Hear the man Paul, decades earlier, warning the Ephesian elders of exactly this. "I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them" (Acts 20:29–30). From among your own selves. Not the pagan outside the wall. The teacher inside the circle. Jude is writing the letter Paul said someone would have to write.

**They crept in, and that is the whole horror**

Then Jude names how it happened, and the verb is the wound. "For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ" (Jude 4). Crept in. Unnoticed. They did not break down the door. They were welcomed through it. They sat in the pew, they led the study, they prayed the prayer, and no one saw. The church that fears the wolf at the gate is undone by the man already at the table.

Watch precisely what they did, because Jude is exact. They perverted grace into sensuality. They took the most beautiful word in the gospel — grace, unearned, free, the cross paying what I could never pay — and turned it into a permission slip. Grace covers it, so do as you please. This is the oldest counterfeit. Paul named it: "I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel" (Galatians 1:6–7). A different gospel that uses the same words. And Peter saw the same men coming: "there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them" (2 Peter 2:1). Secretly. Bringing in. The same creeping.

I have to stop here and say what is uncomfortable to say from a pulpit. I have preached grace as a comfort and watched a man take it as a license, and I did not always have the courage to follow up. It is easier to announce that grace is free than to say, in the same breath, that grace that leaves a man exactly as it found him was never grace at all. Cheap grace is the church's own invention, sold across our own counter, and we did the selling. The false teacher did not have to smuggle in a foreign idea. He only had to take ours and remove the cross from it.

**Contend — and contend for what you did not make**

So Jude gives the church a verb, and it is a hard one. Contend. The word is athletic, the word for a man straining in a contest he might lose. Not defend at a comfortable distance — contend, up close, with effort, with something at stake. But look at what he tells them to contend for. "The faith that was once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 3). Once for all. Delivered. Handed down. It is not a faith we built and may renovate. It is a deposit we received and must guard.

This is the part that implicates me before it implicates anyone teaching error. I do not get to contend for the faith I prefer. I contend for the faith that was handed to me, the one that costs me my preferences, the one that tells me my sensuality is not covered by grace but crucified by it. The men Jude opposes wanted a faith they could edit. So do I, on a Tuesday, when the received word stands across the room from the life I want to live. The line between Jude and the men he names is not intelligence or sincerity. It is submission. Will I guard what was given, or improve it until it fits me.

And here is why the guarding is even possible. Read the first verse you skipped past in your hurry to the warning. They are "those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ" (Jude 1). Kept. The very first thing Jude says about these embattled believers is not that they are strong. It is that they are kept. He will end the whole letter on that word — the God who is able to keep you from stumbling — and he plants it here at the start, before he ever says contend. We do not contend to become kept. We contend because we already are. The grip that holds you is not yours.

The letter he did not want to write is the letter the church most needs. Not because the danger is interesting, but because the danger is in the room, wearing our words, using our grace. He set down the warm letter and picked up the hard one. Some pastor in your life will have to do the same. Some of you will have to do it across your own kitchen table.

Defend the faith you received.

## What Judgment Has Already Done
*The verdict was settled long before the sentence is carried out*

**Text:** Jude 5–16 · **Supporting:** Numbers 14:29–30 · Genesis 19:24–25 · 2 Peter 2:9 · Genesis 4:8

The most dangerous lie a sinner ever believes is that nothing has happened yet. That the account is open, the page is blank, the verdict is still out. Jude writes to people surrounded by men who live exactly as if that were true — and he answers them not with a threat about the future but with a record of the past.

**Three times God has already judged the ungodly**

Jude does not argue that God will judge. He shows that God has, and he stacks the proof. "Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe" (Jude 5). Start there. The same people He saved, He afterward destroyed — the generation rescued from Pharaoh that died in the wilderness for unbelief. "Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness... not one shall come into the land" (Numbers 14:29–30). Rescue is not the same as the end of the story. Being brought out of Egypt did not guarantee being brought into the land. Jude is dismantling the false teacher's deepest comfort: I'm in, so I'm safe.

Then the angels. "And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day" (Jude 6). Even heavenly power, when it abandons its given place, is bound and held. Position does not exempt. Proximity to glory does not exempt.

Then the cities. "Just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire" (Jude 7). "Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire... and he overthrew those cities" (Genesis 19:24–25). Three witnesses, three eras, one verdict. The redeemed who fell, the angels who left, the cities that burned. Peter draws the same conclusion plainly: "the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment" (2 Peter 2:9). Until. The unrighteous are not awaiting a trial. They are already under guard, awaiting a sentence.

This is the reframe the whole letter turns on. Judgment is not a possibility on the horizon. It is a fact in the past with a date still to come. The men troubling the church live in the gap between the verdict and the sentence, and they mistake the delay for acquittal.

**Read them by their fruit, not their words**

Then Jude turns from history to the men in the room, and he refuses to judge them by their doctrine alone. He judges them by their lives. "Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones" (Jude 8). Defile, reject, blaspheme. Watch the sequence — it is always the same. First the appetite is indulged. Then authority is rejected, because authority is the only thing standing between the appetite and its object. Then God Himself is mocked, because a God who judges is an inconvenience to a man committed to his desire.

He reaches back further, to the first murder, the first religious resentment. "Woe to them. For they walked in the way of Cain" (Jude 11). The way of Cain is worship on my own terms, and rage when it is not accepted. "Cain rose up against his brother Abel, and killed him" (Genesis 4:8). The man who will not submit his worship will eventually destroy the brother whose worship was accepted. Jude saw that pattern alive in his own church.

Then the portrait sharpens, and it is merciless and exact. "These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage" (Jude 16). Read that slowly, because it is not a stranger. They grumble. They are never content. They follow their own desires and call it freedom. They boast. They flatter the powerful to gain advantage. There is not one of those marks I cannot find in myself by Thursday. I have grumbled and called it discernment. I have flattered a man I needed and called it kindness. I have followed my own desire and dressed it in the language of calling. The false teacher is not an alien species. He is a man who stopped resisting the things I resist on my better days, and the only thing separating us is grace I did not generate.

**The verdict already stands — and so does the cross**

Here is what should sober every one of us before it sobers anyone else. Jude says these men "long ago were designated for this condemnation" (Jude 4), and now he proves the principle from three thousand years of history. God has done this before. The fruit you indulge today is not awaiting a verdict. It sits under one. The delay you are reading as permission is mercy you are spending on more sin.

And that is exactly why the cross is the only door out of this chapter. If judgment were merely future, you could outrun it with better behavior. But the verdict is already settled, already in the past tense, already true of the ungodly — and the only escape from a settled verdict is for someone to bear it in your place. Jesus, who saved a people out of Egypt and afterward destroyed the unbelieving, is the same Lord who took the sulfur and fire of judgment into His own body on the cross. The God who has already judged the ungodly has already, on the same principle, borne that judgment for everyone who will stop relying on their dreams and rely on Him instead. The settled verdict is the worst news in the letter and the reason the gospel is the best.

So do not read this chapter as a warning about other men. Read it as a record of what God has done, and then turn around and find your own face in verse 16. The men under judgment are not a different kind of human. They are men who believed nothing had happened yet.

God has judged the ungodly before.

## Kept
*Everything you must do, and the One who actually does it*

**Text:** Jude 17–25 · **Supporting:** 2 Peter 3:3 · Philippians 1:6 · John 10:28–29 · Colossians 1:22

A letter that began in alarm ends in worship. That is the most important sentence I can say about Jude, and the church that only hears the warning has not finished reading the letter. He spends most of his words on danger and ends every word on glory — not because the danger was overstated, but because the danger was never the last word over the people of God.

**Remember — the scoffers are not a surprise**

First, Jude steadies the church's nerve. "But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, 'In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions'" (Jude 17–18). The scoffers are not evidence that the gospel has failed. They are evidence that the apostles told the truth. Peter said exactly this: "scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires" (2 Peter 3:3). The presence of the mocker does not unsettle the faith. It confirms it. A church that expected only sunshine panics at the first cloud; a church that was warned keeps its feet.

**Four verbs for the embattled church**

Then Jude gives the church its work, and it is real work, four verbs that demand everything. "But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life" (Jude 20–21). Build. Pray. Keep. Wait. He does not tell a threatened church to retreat. He tells it to grow — to build itself up on the very faith the false teachers are trying to tear down. He does not tell it to fall silent. He tells it to pray in the Spirit. He does not tell it to drift. He tells it to keep itself in the love of God.

And then he turns the church outward, toward the very people the false teachers have endangered. "And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh" (Jude 22–23). Mercy for the wavering. Rescue for the perishing. Mercy mixed with fear for the ones nearest the flame. This is not a church circling its wagons. It is a church running into the fire after the people the wolves left bleeding. Contending for the faith and showing mercy to the doubter are not opposites in Jude. They are the same obedience.

I have to confess where I fail this exactly. I am quick to contend and slow to have mercy on those who doubt. It is easier to fight the teacher than to sit with the half-convinced young believer whose questions embarrass me. Jude will not let me choose. The same paragraph that says snatch them from the fire says have mercy on those who doubt, and the man who only does the snatching and never the mercy has obeyed half a verse and called it faithfulness.

**He is able — and the whole letter has been leaning toward this**

And then Jude does the thing that turns the whole letter inside out. He has just handed the church four commands and three works of mercy — build, pray, keep, wait, have mercy, snatch, fear — enough labor to exhaust any honest believer who knows his own weakness. And the moment you feel the weight of all you must do, Jude turns from your effort to God's power. "Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy" (Jude 24).

Keep yourselves in the love of God, he said in verse 21. He is able to keep you from stumbling, he says in verse 24. The same word. The command and the power. You keep yourself — and the only reason you can is that He is keeping you. This is not a contradiction. It is the gospel's grammar. "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). The work I am commanded to do is the work He guarantees to finish. Jesus said it without a crack of daylight: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand" (John 10:28–29). Jude told us to snatch others from the fire — because no one can snatch us from the hand.

Look at what He is able to do. Not merely keep you from stumbling — "present you blameless before the presence of his glory." Blameless. The word Paul uses for the impossible thing the cross accomplishes: "he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him" (Colossians 1:22). The men of this letter perverted grace into a license to sin. Jude ends by showing what grace actually does — it does not leave you in your sin with a permission slip. It carries you all the way home and sets you before the throne without a stain, with great joy. The false teacher offered grace that excuses you here. The true gospel offers grace that keeps you to the end and presents you there.

The faith you were told to contend for in verse 3 is not finally held by your grip. It is held by His. You contend because you are kept, not in order to be kept. And the letter that opened by calling you "kept for Jesus Christ" (Jude 1) closes by naming the One who does the keeping: "to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever" (Jude 25).

So build, and pray, and keep, and wait, and run into the fire after the doubting — and do all of it as a man already held. The danger was real. The verdict on the ungodly is real. And over the trembling, contending, mercy-bearing church stands a God who has never yet dropped one of His own and will not start with you.

He is able to keep you.
